candidates.attacker_control: The attacker controls the request target. A request such as `GET /%ZZ` (literal `<`/`>` are not rejected by Netty's request-line parsing) with `Accept: text/html` makes FileHandler.decodeComponent throw IllegalArgumentException whose message contains the raw path, and a `:token` route reaches TokenPathBinder.decodeURIComponent, which throws InvalidPathEncodingException wrapping a message that also contains the raw token value including literal HTML.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked that DefaultProductionErrorHandler renders no body (so no production XSS); verified the same class escapes the heading, meta keys/values, page title and stack frames, so line 84 is an isolated omission rather than a uniform unescaped template; verified DEV-mode selection in ServerRegistry; verified Request.getPath()/TokenPathBinder do not validate or sanitize characters before the exception is raised; verified production-path egress and redirect handling rely on Netty header validation (no CRLF injection found there); confirmed the finding could also be a long-standing upstream defect rather than a snapshot-specific modification (no upstream copy or git history is available in this run), and that it is a source-level lead, not a runtime-confirmed exploit.
candidates.impact: Reflected cross-site scripting (same-origin script execution) in the default development error page. A page visitor (developer/operator) can be made to execute attacker script in the dev origin: session/CSRF-token theft for that origin, actions as the viewing user, and pivot into developer tooling. Scope limitation: development mode only (production error handler sends an empty 500 body), so this is not a production-default XSS.
candidates.prerequisites: Server running in development mode (ServerRegistry selects DefaultDevelopmentErrorHandler when ServerConfig.isDevelopment()); a handler that decodes a malformed percent escape from the request path (static `files` handler or any path-token binding); attacker can reach the dev server and negotiate an HTML response (Accept: text/html). Production deployments use DefaultProductionErrorHandler and are not affected by this sink.
candidates.root_cause: ErrorPageRenderer.throwable() emits the exception message with w.println(throwable.toString()) without the BodyWriter.escape() helper used for every other dynamic value in the class (cause prefix, stack frames, headings, meta keys/values, page title). Exception messages produced by built-in request-path decoding echo raw attacker-supplied request data, turning the dev error page into an HTML injection sink.
candidates.title: Reflected XSS via unescaped exception message in the default development error page
candidates.trace: Request → FileHandler.handle (decodeComponent) or TokenPathBinder.bind (decodeURIComponent) throws IllegalArgumentException/InvalidPathEncodingException whose message embeds the raw attacker path → DefaultContext.next wraps it in HandlerException (message = cause.toString()) → execution onError unwraps HandlerException to its cause (DefaultContext.start) → DefaultContext.error forwards to ServerErrorHandler → DefaultDevelopmentErrorHandler.error → byContent(...).html(...) → ErrorPageRenderer.throwable → `w.println(throwable.toString())` unescaped → response sent as text/html (HTML_UTF_8).
candidates.unverified: No runtime execution, browser PoC, or upstream diff was possible in this run. Exploitability depends on the application running in development mode, on a reachable code path that produces an exception message containing the payload, and on the request surviving Netty's request-line parsing with literal `<`/`>` characters. Whether this is the benchmark's intended defect or an upstream long-standing issue is unverified.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-79 Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

coverage_summary: Scope: the full assigned tree is 947 files (947 model-visible; 748 parsed Java files; index omits 48 files and reports 1 parse error, no control/data-flow resolution). I reviewed the main request-processing chain end-to-end (NettyHandlerAdapter, DefaultRequest/DefaultResponse, DefaultResponseTransmitter, RequestBody, DefaultContext, path/FileSystemBinding/FileHandler, redirector/public-address), sessions (SessionModule, CookieBasedSessionId, DefaultSession, ClientSideSessionStore/Crypto/Signer, redis store), ratpack-pac4j auth, groovy/handlebars/thymeleaf/thymeleaf3/rocker template renderers and template resolution, HTTP client (RequestConfig/RequestActionSupport/DefaultHttpClient), TLS setup/deserializers, config sources, error handlers/renderers, health/metrics, jdbc-tx, consul, spring-boot, remote, gson, retrofit2, site, and build/plugin sources at a lighter level. Files whose content is minified JavaScript or generated documentation were searched but not line-reviewed. No tests exist in the snapshot, so dynamic confirmation was not possible.
limitations: No upstream reference (git history, fixed version, or patch) is available in this run, so I could not distinguish a snapshot-specific modification from a long-standing upstream defect for the selected candidate or the rejected leads.

The P1 relation index is syntactic only (no data flow, semantic resolution, or reachability) and omits 48 files; index labels were used only for navigation and every candidate edge was checked against source text.
No runtime execution, tests, scanners, or exploit payloads were run; all statements are source-level analysis and the candidate is not runtime-confirmed.
The selected finding is scoped to development mode (default development error handler); production behavior differs (empty 500 body).

Large areas (ratpack-exec stream internals, Rx/Reactor/Hystrix/NewRelic/Rocker/Gradle plugin logic) were reviewed only at a high level, and markdown/manual/minified JS assets were not security-audited.
I could not verify whether the unescaped exception output is exploitable with every servlet path/encoding combination (Netty request-line acceptance of literal '<'/'>' was not executed).

rejected_leads.lead: ClientSideSessionConfig.secretToken defaults to Long.toString(System.currentTimeMillis() / 10000) (ratpack-session/.../ClientSideSessionConfig.java:29), used as HMAC key in ClientSideSessionModule.signer (lines 127-132); a captured cookie allows offline brute-force of the key over plausible boot times and forging of signed client-side session cookies (session forgery / possible privilege escalation).
rejected_leads.reason: High-impact, but the class javadoc explicitly documents this default ('If not set, this is set to a time based value'), so it reads as an intended (insecure-default) configuration choice rather than a concrete code defect; classified as a hardening/design weakness rather than the strongest source-evidence candidate.

rejected_leads.lead: RatpackPac4j.requireAuth treats a null authorizer as authorized: all(authorizerList, a -> a == null || a.isAuthorized(webContext, userProfile)) (ratpack-pac4j/.../RatpackPac4j.java:214), contradicting the method javadoc that each authorizer must return true.
rejected_leads.reason: Fail-open authorization logic, but not attacker-reachable: the null must be supplied by application code when constructing the handler; no request-controlled input can make an Authorizer element null, so no external attacker path exists.

rejected_leads.lead: Default PublicAddress infers host from X-Forwarded-Host/Host and scheme from X-Forwarded-Proto/X-Forwarded-Ssl (InferringPublicAddress.java:91-112, wired by ServerRegistry.java:101-104); DefaultRedirector then builds Location from it (DefaultRedirector.java:61-77), enabling open redirect / host-header poisoning for apps doing relative redirects.
rejected_leads.reason: Attacker-reachable in default configuration, but the behavior is explicitly documented on PublicAddress.inferred(), and a ConstantPublicAddress override exists (publicAddress config), so this is an accepted upstream trust assumption rather than a clear defect; left as a hardening lead.

rejected_leads.lead: ratpack-remote RemoteControlHandler executes Groovy commands sent by any HTTP client without authentication (ratpack-remote/.../RemoteControlHandler.java, RatpackReceiver.java).
rejected_leads.reason: Executes attacker-supplied code by design for development/test remoting; the decorator is not wired anywhere by default in this snapshot (verified no usage outside the module), so it is an intentional dangerous feature, not an injected defect.

rejected_leads.lead: File serving traversal: TODO in FileSystemBindingHandler.java:46 ('validate the path isn't escaping up with ../') plus FileHandler decoding of the past-binding.
rejected_leads.reason: Verified counterevidence: DefaultFileSystemBinding.file() strips a leading slash, normalizes, and enforces startsWith(binding)/dummy-binding containment (lines 47-71); FileHandler decodes only once and file() re-validates, so `..`/absolute/encoded-slash traversal is blocked. The TODO is stale.

rejected_leads.lead: Client-side session readability without secretKey, missing cookie Secure/SameSite defaults, dev-mode stack-trace disclosure, Weak MD5 checksummer, thread-local request-id random.
rejected_leads.reason: Hardening opportunities or non-security uses (MD5 checksummer is for cache-busting; request ids are not security tokens); none meets the evidence threshold for a vulnerability candidate.

summary: Reviewed the assigned Ratpack snapshot (947 files; 748 parsed Java files; P1 relation index partial, no data-flow capability) with emphasis on request handling, path binding/static files, session handling, pac4j auth, template engines, HTTP client, TLS, config loading and integration modules. After tracing attacker-controlled request data through the framework's sinks, the single strongest candidate is a reflected-XSS sink in the default development error page: ErrorPageRenderer writes Throwable.toString() into the HTML page unescaped, while every other dynamic value in the same class is escaped. Attacker-influenced strings reach exception messages on several built-in paths (malformed percent-escapes in the request path/tokens are echoed verbatim by FileHandler.decodeComponent and TokenPathBinder.decodeURIComponent), and that message is rendered as HTML when the client negotiates text/html. Several plausible leads were examined and rejected (listed below); the finding is a lead, not a runtime-confirmed vulnerability.
